title: About the margin inspector
body:
This little panel checks that the chart you just made will be easy to measure.

Many spectrophotometers (like the i1Pro or ColorMunki) are slid along the printed chart by hand, often in a ruler or holder (sometimes called a jig or rig). For that to work, the coloured patches need a bit of blank white paper around them — if a patch sits too close to the edge of the page, the instrument can run off the paper or bump the ruler, and the reading fails. This panel helps you catch that before you print.

What the numbers mean:
• Left, Right, Top, Bottom — how much white space there is between each edge of the paper and the first PATCH, shown in both millimetres and inches.

  These can read larger than the margins you set, and usually should. Two things sit in that space on purpose. Some charts print row indicators down the left and strip letters across the top, so you can find one patch among hundreds — that lettering needs room. And patches come in whole units, so the grid almost never divides the width exactly; the leftover is shared at both ends to keep the block centred on the page. Neither is the app ignoring your margins: they are the smallest white border you asked for, and this panel reports what the patches actually got.
• Patch width — how wide one patch is across a strip.
• Strip length — how long each strip of patches is (handy because some jigs have a maximum, e.g. 240 mm for the i1Pro).

The 'min' column is the smallest each margin should be for your ruler or jig. If a margin is below its minimum, that row turns red and a short warning appears; when everything is fine you'll see a friendly green 'Margins: OK'.

You decide those minimums yourself: open Preferences → Instrument Margins and set them for each instrument and paper size (the starting values are sensible defaults you can adjust to your own ruler). They're only a helpful warning — you can always go ahead and print anyway.

The three tick boxes below draw these numbers onto the preview in different w

title: Instrument-margin guide lines
body:
Draws the minimum margins your instrument needs straight onto the preview, as short dotted lines — one for each edge of the paper.

Use it to see at a glance whether the patches keep far enough from the edges: a patch area that stays inside all four dotted lines is good to go. A line is black where that margin is fine and red where it is too tight, so a problem edge finds you rather than the other way round.

You also get a thin solid rectangle marking the true edge of the sheet, because the page is drawn slightly inside the preview's white border — a 0 mm margin would sit right on that line.

The minimums are yours to set: Preferences → Instrument Margins, per instrument and paper size.

Default: off.

title: Margin guide lines
body:
Draws a long dotted line at each of the four margins ChromIQ has just MEASURED — right where the patch area meets the white paper.

This is the double-check for the numbers above: if the Left figure says 8.0 mm, this line shows you where those 8 mm end. It is a different thing from the instrument-margin lines above, which show what your ruler NEEDS rather than what the chart HAS — and you can have both sets on at once to compare them.

Default: off.

title: Measurement coordinates on pointer
body:
Turns your mouse into a ruler.

Tick it and wherever you move the pointer over the chart, a thin cross-hair marks the exact spot and its position is shown next to it — measured from the top-left corner of the PAPER itself, not the preview's outer edge. The top line is millimetres to one decimal, the line below it inches to three.

It is the easiest way to check a real distance on screen: hover over the edge of a patch, or over a margin, and read off exactly where it sits.

Default: off.

title: About chart layout information
body:
This panel shows the SIZE and SHAPE of your chart — how many colour patches it has, how they're arranged, and how many pages it needs — so you can judge a chart before (and after) you make it.

What the rows mean:
• Total patches — how many colour squares the whole chart holds. More patches usually means a more accurate profile, but a bigger chart to print and measure.
• … of those, fill-up — how many of the total are paper-white fill-up patches. Measuring instruments read whole strips, so when your designed patches don't fill the last strip exactly, it is topped up with plain paper-white patches (Argyll's printtarg does the same). That's why the total can be a little higher than the number of patches you designed — for example 896 designed becoming 910 printed. The fill-up patches are measured like any others and are harmless; nothing of yours is lost or changed.
• Patches per strip — how many patches sit in one strip (a strip is a single column the instrument reads from top to bottom).
• Strips (this page) — how many of those strips fit across the page you're looking at.
• Pages — how many sheets the chart spans.
• Patch size — how big each patch is (width × height in mm). With “Prioritise chart area” this is worked out for you; very small patches can be hard for the instrument to read.

The two columns:
• on screen — the real numbers of the chart currently in the preview.
• estimate — what the settings you have right now would produce if you generate. This is shown while the ChromIQ layout engine is switched on, because the engine can work the layout out exactly in advance.

Change a setting (patch size, paper, margins, alignment…) and the estimate updates live. Any number that would come out different from the chart on screen turns amber — so you can see the effect of a change before re-generating the chart.

Hexagonal patches have two heights, and they are not the same number.

title: Step 1 — Make a test chart
body:
This is where you design the sheet of colour patches your printer will print. The patches are how ChromIQ later "learns" how your printer reproduces colour.

Before you start:
• Pick the printer and paper you actually want to profile — the profile will only be accurate for that exact combination.
• Have a rough idea of how careful you want to be. More patches = more accuracy, but also more ink and paper.

First, name your profiling project.
The "Printer profile project name" field at the top is the name of this whole job. It becomes the project folder, every file ChromIQ makes along the way (chart, measurements, ICC profile) and the name written inside the profile itself — so what you see later in, say, macOS ColorSync Utility matches the folder exactly. A good name describes the printer, the paper and the quality, e.g. Canon_Pro1000_PhotoRagBaryta_i1Pro3_High. Change your mind? Just edit the name — ChromIQ offers to rename the folder and files to match (until the profile has been built, after which you copy it to a new name instead). Your work is saved automatically; there's no Save button to remember.

Coming back to a profile later?
Click “Open Project” at the top left of the window — the first of the three small buttons beside the ChromIQ logo — to reopen a profile you started before. Its chart, measurements and any finished profile are all exactly where you left them. It asks for the profile's "project.json" file inside your ChromIQ folder.

You have three ways to make a chart — from quickest to most hands-on:

☰  Built-in presets — the presets button in the header, top right (its icon looks like a small list).
Click it to open a little menu of ready-made, professionally tuned charts, grouped by the measuring instrument they're made for (i1Pro or ColorMunki). Pick one and ChromIQ drops the finished chart straight into your profile — under the name you chose above, without changing it — so there are no settings to understand and nothing to get wrong. This is the

title: Measurement Instrument
body:
Tells the chart generator which spectrophotometer you will use to read the printed chart. The patch grid is built around that instrument's strip width, patch size and spacing — so getting this right is essential.

  •  i1Pro / i1Pro 2 / i1Pro 3 — handheld strip reader, the most common choice. Reads a column of patches in one sweep.

  •  i1Pro 3 Plus — larger-aperture version of the i1Pro 3. Reads bigger patches, so far fewer fit per sheet (~5× less than the regular i1Pro).

  •  ColorMunki / i1Studio / ColorChecker Studio — entry-level device. Reads one patch at a time on its own; with the optional measuring rig it pairs them up (see the Double Density option).

  •  SpectroScan — flatbed XY scanner. A motorised arm reads each patch individually, so it packs far more colours per sheet than any strip reader.

Picking the wrong instrument produces a chart your device cannot align to or read reliably — you'll see "patches not found" or alignment errors when measuring.

In Guided mode the layout adapts to this choice automatically.

  •  CR30 (ChnSpec) — a small hand-held colorimeter that reads ONE patch at a time. You put it on a patch, press the button on the instrument, and ChromIQ records that patch and highlights the next one. The chart is a plain grid of squares with row indicators and column letters so you can always find the patch being asked for.

     Two things to know before you choose it. Its patch size is PROVISIONAL — 12 mm squares, a reasoned starting point rather than a measured minimum — so make them larger if you find yourself missing patches. And every patch is a hand placement and a button press of about two seconds, so a full A4 sheet of around 345 patches takes well over ten minutes. Pick a patch count you are happy to sit through.

     A CR30 chart is always laid out by ChromIQ's own layout engine, and can only be read by ChromIQ — standard ArgyllCMS chartread does not know this instrument and will refuse the chart.

title: Double Density (-h)
body:
Doubles the number of patches that fit in each measurement strip when using a ColorMunki / i1Studio / ColorChecker Studio.

REQUIRES the physical measuring rig accessory — a clear plastic guide that mounts the instrument over the chart. Without the rig the device cannot align to the tighter patch spacing and will misread.

With the rig you get roughly twice as many patches per page, which means either a more detailed profile from the same number of sheets, or the same profile quality on fewer sheets. Recommended for anyone with the rig — it's a strict upgrade on patch density.

Has no effect on i1Pro, i1Pro 3 Plus or SpectroScan — the option is hidden when those are selected.

title: Triple Density (i1Pro layout emulation)
body:
ColorMunki + rig only. The chart is generated with the i1Pro strip layout (tighter, smaller patches than a native ColorMunki chart), then the produced .ti2 is rewritten so chartread still talks to your ColorMunki. Result: roughly 3× the patch count of a plain ColorMunki chart at the same paper size — a more detailed profile from the same number of sheets, or the same profile quality on far fewer sheets.

REQUIRES the physical measuring rig accessory. Without the rig the ColorMunki cannot track the tighter i1-style strips.

Mutually exclusive with Double density — pick one or the other.

Has no effect on i1Pro, i1Pro 3 Plus or SpectroScan — the option is hidden when those are selected.

title: Paper Size
body:
Sets the dimensions of each sheet in the printed chart. The chart always fills the page edge to edge — bigger paper fits more patches, which means a more detailed profile from fewer sheets.

Pick the same size you will actually print on, including its orientation. Strip readers (i1Pro family) read top-to-bottom, so:

  •  Portrait — longer strips, fewer of them. Standard choice.

  •  Landscape — shorter strips, more of them. Use this when your printer feeds landscape more reliably, or when a portrait sheet would leave the last strip too close to the paper edge.

Some paper sizes are hidden depending on the selected instrument:

  •  A3 Portrait is hidden for i1Pro — the landscape variant fits ~43% more patches.

  •  Small photo formats (5×7", 4×6") are hidden for i1Pro 3 Plus — its large patches don't leave a usable profile on those.

If you change paper size mid-workflow, the recommended patch count and page count update automatically.

title: Number of Pages
body:
How many physical sheets the chart spans. Each sheet is filled with as many patches as fit for the selected paper, instrument and layout — so total patches = patches-per-page × pages.

More pages means more colour samples, which produces a more accurate profile. The trade-off is more ink, more paper and a longer reading session. Rough guide:

  •  1 page — quick check or single-sheet workflows (~500 patches on A4 with an i1Pro). Fine for casual profiling.

  •  2-3 pages — recommended for everyday photo printing. Good balance of accuracy versus effort.

  •  4-5+ pages — professional or fine-art workflows where the profile needs to nail tricky tonal transitions and out-of-gamut colours.

How many patches you actually need depends on your printer's colour gamut, ink set and how non-linear it behaves. When in doubt, more is better.

title: Suppress Left Clip Border (-L)
body:
Removes the left-edge paper-clip border, gaining ~15 mm for extra patches.
Enable unless you use a physical page-clamp jig.  Recommended: ON.

title: Don't Limit Strip Length (-P)
body:
Removes printtarg's built-in strip-length cap (~250 mm) so each measurement strip runs full-bleed across the paper.

Why it helps:
On larger papers (A2, A3+, 11×17, Legal, A3-landscape) the cap ends strips early — well before the page edge — and printtarg rebalances the layout to keep strips equal-length. With -P the strips can use the full paper width/height, so noticeably more patches fit per sheet — up to ~2.5× more on A2, smaller gains on A4 (where the cap barely bit anyway).

Trade-off:
Long strips take longer to read in one sweep. Most i1Pro / i1Pro 3 / i1Pro 3 Plus users will be fine — modern hardware tracks long strips reliably. If you have an older instrument that struggles with strips near the paper edge, leave this off.

Only affects i1Pro family strip readers. Hidden for ColorMunki (per-patch reader) and SpectroScan (XY flatbed) — -P has no effect on either layout.

title: Refinement Profile (Pre-conditioning)
body:
Use this to make a second, noticeably better profile after you have already built and confirmed a working one for the same printer + paper.

How it helps:
Your first profile tells ChromIQ which colours your printer gets right and which it struggles with. When you turn this option on, ChromIQ uses that knowledge to place the new test patches more cleverly — sampling more in the regions your printer reproduces least accurately, and fewer in the regions it already nails. The end result is a profile that is more accurate where it matters, without needing more patches overall.

When to use it:
• You already have a first ICC profile (.icc or .icm) built from this same printer + paper combination.
• You want to invest one more round of printing and measuring to get a noticeably better profile, especially for tricky papers (matte, baryta, fine-art).

When NOT to use it:
• On a first-ever profile for this paper — leave this off and just build the normal way.
• If you don't have a working profile yet for this exact paper/printer.

Tip: the more pages you print on the refinement pass, the more benefit the cleverer patch placement gives you.

title: Printer profile project name
body:
The name of this whole profiling project — think of it as the job's title. It becomes the project folder on disk, the base name of every file ChromIQ makes along the way (chart, measurements, the finished ICC profile) and the profile's own embedded description — so what you see later in, for example, macOS ColorSync Utility matches the folder and files exactly.

(The “printer profile” itself is the .icc / .icm file this project produces at the end. Naming the project after the printer and paper keeps that file easy to recognise.)

Choose a name that identifies this printer and paper at a glance. A good name describes the printer (name or abbreviation), the paper (type/id and substrate such as glossy or matte), the colour space, the measurement instrument and the profile quality — e.g. Canon_Pro1000_PhotoRagBaryta_RGB_i1Pro3_High. Use underscores or dashes instead of spaces.

You can rename it later: change the name here and ChromIQ offers to rename the folder and files to match — until the profile has been built, after which you copy it to a new name instead.

title: Run Description
body:
Optional, and empty unless you fill it in.

A project usually holds several runs, and they are easy to confuse once there are a few. This is where you say what makes this one different: the paper, the finish, the chart size, or whatever you vary. It is only a description — it does not change any file name.

Many people find it easiest to settle on a pattern and stick to it. For example, with the project named for the printer, paper make, size and instrument:

    Printer profile project name:  Canon_Pro1000_Hahnemuehle_A4_i1Pro
    Run 1 Description:  PhotoRagBaryta_Glossy_Large
    Run 2 Description:  PhotoRagBaryta_Glossy_Small
    Run 3 Description:  PhotoRagBaryta_Matte_Large

Whatever you type here is added to the end of the profile's own description in the tab where you build the profile — that tab is called “4. Build Profile”, or “4. Calibration & Profiling” when calibration options are switched on in Preferences — so the finished .icc carries it too. Unless you have written your own description there, which is never overwritten.

THIS STAYS WITH THE RUN. Restoring an earlier chart with “Restore Used Chart” does not change it, because it describes the run and not the sheet of paper.

title: Create Chart for Calibration
body:
Use this before running printcal to create a printer linearisation curve.

When enabled:
  • Output files are prefixed with 'cal_' (e.g. cal_MyChart.ti1)
  • Patch count is set to 0 (auto), white and black patches set to 0
  • Single channel steps set to 20, randomisation disabled
  • Good distribution (-G) is disabled

Generate the chart, print it, and measure it. The resulting cal_*.ti3
file is automatically routed to the Create Calibration File module
in the Calibration & Profiling tab.

Existing cal_* files in your working folder are preserved when this
option is OFF, so your .cal file survives the next chart generation.

title: Chart Notes
body: Optional free-text label stamped onto the right edge of the chart TIFFs alongside the targen and printtarg commands that produced them. Useful for recording the exact printer/paper combination this chart was made for, so you can match it to the right ICC profile months later. Patch pixels are not modified — only the white margin to the right of the patches is stamped.

title: Stamp Commands
body:
Prints the exact settings that produced this chart along its right edge, so the sheet explains itself.

What is stamped depends on how the chart was laid out: with the ChromIQ layout engine it is the targen command and the engine's own layout settings, and with printtarg it is the targen and printtarg command lines. The ChromIQ version is included either way, beside Argyll's own vertical ID line.

WHY YOU MIGHT WANT IT: months later you can read the printed sheet and make exactly the same chart again, without having to remember what you chose.

Switch it off if you would rather keep the right margin clean and print only your own chart notes — or leave the sheet completely unmarked by clearing the notes box as well.

title: Left Clip Info
body:
Fills the wide blank strip on the LEFT side of the chart — the space printtarg reserves for the i1Pro 2 / i1Pro 3 Plus scanning-table clip — with two rotated text columns:

• Outer column: a one-line chart summary (patch count + paper size), a print-driver reminder (borderless, no expansion, retain size, color management off), and a fill-in-the-blank form line for date, printer, ink set, profile name, paper and driver settings.
• Inner column: orientation instructions for the i1Pro scanning table — which edge faces up and how to seat the sheet in the clip.

This option is only available when:
  • The instrument is i1Pro / i1Pro 2 or i1Pro 3 Plus.
  • 'Suppress left clip border' is OFF (so the clip strip is actually reserved).
  • The paper size is A4 / Letter or larger — smaller sheets have no room for legible rotated text.

The row hides automatically when these conditions aren't met. Patch pixels are never modified — only the otherwise-empty left clip strip is stamped.

title: Manual Presets
body:
Save and recall named snapshots of all Manual mode settings.

  +  Save current parameter values as a new named preset.
  −  Delete the currently selected preset.
  ▢  Open this tab's presets folder in Finder.

Select a preset from the dropdown to instantly restore all
values. The Default entry always resets to built-in defaults.

Presets are stored as plain .json files — one per preset —
in a ChromIQ folder under your system's Preferences / AppData
/ config location. Use the folder button (▢) on the right of
the preset row to open it. To share a preset, copy the .json
out of that folder and send it to a colleague; to install a
shared preset, drop the .json into the matching folder on the
target machine and ChromIQ will pick it up on the next launch.

The target name field is not saved with presets.
Presets persist between sessions.

title: ChromIQ layout engine
body:
When ON, ChromIQ builds your test charts itself instead of calling ArgyllCMS printtarg. The engine packs the colour patches more efficiently, can put useful information where printtarg leaves blank space, and lets you fully customise the layout below per instrument and paper. The engine is the default for new charts; printtarg stays one untick away.

When OFF the chart is made by printtarg exactly as before. This switch only affects how charts are CREATED; printing and measuring existing charts always work the same way, so it is safe to switch back at any time.

─────────────────────────────────
What each one gives you
─────────────────────────────────

Only with the ChromIQ engine:
  • more patches on every sheet
  • you choose the patch size
  • you choose each margin separately
  • the instrument's own margins are enforced
  • spacer size and colour are yours to set
  • notes and a record area printed on the sheet
  • a clip border to cut along
  • multi-ink (CMY+N) charts
  • the layout is saved with the chart and can be reopened
  • the live patch preview while measuring
  • scanner-target geometry
  • reading-pace guidance (with the reading engine too)

The same either way:
  • the chart is read and profiled identically
  • every ArgyllCMS tool accepts it unchanged

Both produce a chart ArgyllCMS reads and profiles in exactly the same way — the difference is what the sheet looks like and how much you can decide about it.

title: Device Type (-d)
body:
Defines the colorant combination of your output device.

Print spaces are subtractive: device value 0 = white (no ink),
maximum = black (full ink).  Video/display spaces are additive:
device value 0 = black, maximum = white.

Common choices:
  • Print grey (-d 0)  — single-channel greyscale printer
  • Video grey (-d 1)  — single-channel display/monitor
  • Print RGB (-d 2)   — standard RGB inkjet (default, recommended)
  • Video RGB (-d 3)   — RGB display/monitor
  • CMYK (-d 4)        — four-colour inkjet or offset press
  • CMY (-d 5)         — three-colour, no separate black channel

Options 6–15 are for specialty multi-channel inkjet printers with
additional inks (light cyan/magenta, orange, green, violet, etc.).
Use -D (Expert) to fine-tune the colorant set if needed.

title: Total Patch Count (-f)
body:
Sets the total number of colour patches.  More patches = better
profile accuracy but longer print and measurement time.
Typical ranges for RGB inkjet:
  • Quick test: 400–600
  • Standard:   800–1200
  • High quality: 1500–2000
  • Very high:  2500–3000

Auto (next to the spinbox): when ticked, the patch count is
computed live from the chosen paper, instrument, double-density,
left-border, patch scale, margin, and the Pages spinbox in the
printtarg section — picking the largest value that fills exactly
that many sheets with no empty space.  The spinbox is greyed out
while Auto is on and shows the current estimate.  For custom
layouts (non-default patch scale or margin) Auto runs a short
binary search against targen, so the value may take a second
to update.

In Guided mode this is computed automatically from the
patches-per-page database × selected page count.
Set to 0 in Guided mode to use automatic calculation.

title: White Patches (-e)
body:
How many pure paper-white patches to add to the chart. The
instrument measures these to learn exactly how white your paper
is, which anchors the bright end of the profile. 4 is a good
default; very glossy papers can benefit from a few more.

Auto (checkbox):
Turn on "Auto" and ChromIQ picks this number for you, based on
how many patches the whole chart holds — so a small one-page
chart gets a few white patches and a big multi-page chart gets
more, without you having to think about it.

How the Auto number is worked out:
  • A chart of about 560 patches gets 4 white patches.
  • Every time the chart roughly doubles in size, the count
    grows by 50 % (4 → 6 → 8 …).
  • It never goes above 8 (more than that just wastes space)
    and never below 2.

When Auto is on, this box is greyed out and shows "Auto". Turn
it off any time to type your own number.

title: Black Patches (-B)
body:
How many maximum-ink (device black) patches to add to the chart.
The instrument measures these to learn the darkest tone your
printer can produce, which anchors the shadow end of the profile.
4 is a good default for RGB printers.

Auto (checkbox):
Turn on "Auto" and ChromIQ picks this number for you, based on
how many patches the whole chart holds — a small chart gets a
few black patches, a big chart gets more.

How the Auto number is worked out:
  • A chart of about 560 patches gets 4 black patches.
  • Every time the chart roughly doubles in size, the count
    grows by 50 % (4 → 6 → 8 …).
  • It never goes above 8 and never below 2.

When Auto is on, this box is greyed out and shows "Auto". Turn
it off any time to type your own number.

title: Grey Axis Steps (-g)
body:
Extra neutral grey patches placed evenly from white to black.
These help the profile reproduce greys cleanly, without colour
casts — important for black-and-white photos and neutral tones.
Rough guide if you set it by hand: 0 for a quick profile,
50–100 for a standard one, 128+ for high quality.

Auto (checkbox):
Turn on "Auto" and ChromIQ picks this number for you, scaled to
how many patches the whole chart holds — a bigger chart gets a
longer, finer grey ramp.

How the Auto number is worked out:
  • A chart of about 560 patches gets 32 grey steps.
  • Every time the chart roughly doubles in size, the steps
    double too (32 → 64 → 128).
  • It never goes above 128 and never below 8.

When Auto is on, this box is greyed out and shows "Auto". Turn
it off any time to type your own number.

(Guided mode always sets this automatically using the same idea.)

title: Thorough Optimisation (-G)
body:
Makes targen spend extra time placing the patches as evenly as
possible across your printer's colour gamut. The patch set is
the same kind (OFPS — Optimised Farthest Point Sampling, the
default distribution) either way; this just switches it from
"fast" mode to "good" mode.

Recommended ON for any chart you will actually print and
measure: a few extra seconds of computer time during chart
generation gives you a measurably better profile.

Turn OFF only if you're iterating quickly on chart settings and
don't care about absolute patch quality (e.g. testing print
layouts before committing to a final chart).

Has no effect when "Patch Distribution" is set to anything other
than OFPS — the alternative distributions (random, quasi-random,
body-centered cubic, …) ignore this flag.

title: Single Channel Steps (-s)
body:
Adds extra single-channel ramp patches (R, G, B separately).
Useful for characterising individual ink behaviour.
Typical: 0 for quick, 20–50 for standard, 50–100 for high.

title: Add/Remove Colorant (-D)
body:
Modifies the colorant set established by Device Type (-d) by adding
or removing one individual colorant.  If the chosen colorant is
already present in the set it is removed; if absent it is added.

Typical uses:
  • Add Orange (-D 5) to standard CMYK for extended gamut
  • Add Light Cyan (-D 11) / Light Magenta (-D 12) to CMYK
    for smoother highlight gradients

Enable multiple slots to stack additional colorants (each enabled
slot reveals the next, up to 11 total modifications).

Leave this disabled for standard device types 0–5.

title: Add/Remove Colorant (-D)
body:
Modifies the colorant set established by Device Type (-d) by adding
or removing one individual colorant.  If the chosen colorant is
already present in the set it is removed; if absent it is added.

Typical uses:
  • Add Orange (-D 5) to standard CMYK for extended gamut

title: Pre-conditioning Profile (-c)
body:
An existing ICC profile for this printer/paper combination used
to pre-condition the patch distribution in perceptual space.
Using a previous profile here produces patches more evenly
distributed in the output gamut, leading to better accuracy on
a second profiling pass.  Leave blank for a first-time profile.

title: Calibration Override (-C)
body:
Optional .cal file whose calibration curves are applied when estimating
the ink limit for patch generation.  Overrides any .cal embedded in
the ICC target .ti3 file produced by a previous profiling pass.

Use this when you have a validated device calibration (e.g. from
printcal/applycal) and want targen to account for it when computing
how many patches are needed in the shadow region.

Type "none" in the field (without quotes) to explicitly prevent any
.cal from being used, even if one is embedded in the .ti3.

Leave blank for most workflows — only needed when you are managing
a separate calibration curve independently from the profile.

title: Neutral Axis Steps (-n)
body:
Adds extra wedge patches along the perceptually-true neutral
axis of your printer + paper, as defined by the pre-conditioning
ICC profile loaded via -c.

How it differs from -g (Grey Axis Steps):
  • -g walks RGB device values (R = G = B): 0/0/0, 32/32/32,
    64/64/64 … That assumes equal device values print as a
    neutral grey, which is only true on a perfectly linearised
    printer.  On a real printer the "device grey ramp" usually
    has a colour cast.
  • -n asks the supplied profile: "what RGB values does THIS
    printer actually need to reproduce a neutral L*a*b*
    (a* = b* = 0) patch at each lightness step?"  Those
    (typically non-equal) RGB values get added as patches.

How it differs from -N (Neutral Axis Emphasis):
  • -N is a 0–1 dial that biases the existing OFPS patch
    distribution toward the neutral region.  It does not add
    named steps.
  • -n adds explicit, profile-derived neutral patches on top
    of whatever the rest of the distribution produces.

When to use it:
  • You already have a first-pass ICC profile for this paper
    and you're building a refinement chart.  Load that profile
    under Pre-conditioning Profile (-c), then set -n to 32–64
    to densely characterise the corrected neutral axis.
  • For a first-time chart with no -c, leave this at 0 —
    without a pre-conditioning profile there is no "true"
    neutral axis to sample from, and -g already covers the
    device-space ramp.

Typical refinement values: 32 for routine work, 64 for
fine-art / proofing where neutrality is critical.

Requires -c to be set; has no effect otherwise.

title: Neutral Axis Emphasis (-N)
body:
Controls how strongly patches cluster near the neutral axis.
0.0 = no emphasis, 1.0 = maximum clustering near grey.
Default 0.5 is appropriate for most printers.

title: Dark Region Emphasis (-V)
body:
Adds extra patches in dark (shadow) areas of the gamut.
1.0 = no emphasis (default).  Increase to 2.0–3.0 for printers
with complex shadow behaviour (e.g. matte fine-art papers).

title: Total Ink Limit (-l)
body:
The maximum total amount of ink the printer is allowed to lay
down on the paper, as a percentage. 100 % = one full ink layer,
200 % = two full layers (e.g. 100C + 100K), and so on.

Why it matters (especially for CMYK / CMYK+N):
Without a limit, targen happily generates patches like 100C +
100M + 100Y + 100K = 400 %. That much wet ink can puddle, dry
slowly, mottle, or even tear the paper — and the profile built
from such patches predicts colours your printer can't actually
produce.

How to choose a value:
  • Most CMYK inkjets:        260 – 320 %
  • Coated / glossy papers:   320 – 360 %
  • Newsprint, low-quality:   220 – 260 %
  • Extended-gamut (CMYKOGV): 400 – 500 %  (more inks share
                                           the total budget)

If unsure, check your printer's documentation or paper profile
guidance, or measure: print a small ink-limit test wedge and
pick the highest value that dries cleanly without bleeding.

For RGB workflows: usually leave this disabled — RGB inkjets
handle their own ink limiting internally, so targen doesn't
need to budget across channels.

Tick the checkbox to enable.

title: Patch Distribution (-t / -r / -R / -q / -Q / -i / -I)
body:
How targen decides where to place each colour patch in the
printer's gamut. Different algorithms give different trade-offs
between coverage, evenness, and speed.

Pick ONE. These are mutually exclusive — selecting any of them
replaces the default OFPS placement entirely.

OFPS (default, recommended):
Optimised Farthest Point Sampling. Iteratively places each new
patch as far as possible from every existing patch, producing
the most even coverage of any algorithm here. Slower than the
alternatives but the gold standard for profile quality. Pair
with "Thorough Optimisation (-G)" for best results.

Incremental Far Point (-t):
A simpler farthest-point method. Faster than OFPS, slightly
less even. Use when OFPS is too slow on very large patch counts
and you accept a small quality drop.

Random — device space (-r):
Uniformly random patches in raw device values (e.g. RGB).
Fastest possible, but coverage in *perceived* colour is uneven
— wastes patches in regions our eye barely distinguishes.

Random — perceptual space (-R):
Uniformly random in perceived colour (Lab). Better than -r if
you must use random, since patches are spread evenly by what
the eye sees. Still less optimal than OFPS for the same count.

Quasi-random space-filling (-q / -Q):
Low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol-like) that fill space more
evenly than true random without OFPS's iterative cost.
-q in device space, -Q in perceptual space. A good middle
ground when OFPS is too slow.

Body-centered cubic lattice (-i / -I):
A fixed regular lattice (each patch surrounded by 8 neighbours
in a cube pattern). Deterministic and very even, but inflexible
— exact patch counts that fit the lattice are limited. -i in
device space, -I in perceptual space.

Most users should leave this on OFPS.

title: OFPS Adaptation (-A)
body:
How strongly OFPS bends its even-coverage rule to follow the
shape of a Pre-conditioning Profile (-c). Only meaningful when
OFPS is the chosen Patch Distribution AND a -c profile is set.

0.0 = ignore the profile completely — pure even coverage in
      device space, as if no -c were given.
1.0 = follow the profile fully — concentrate patches where the
      profile says the printer's gamut is interesting (i.e. the
      shape of the actual colour space).

Default in targen is 0.10 (mild) for a first pass and 1.0 when
-c is set; ChromIQ leaves this at 0.10 unless you explicitly
change it so you don't get a surprise behaviour switch.

Increase toward 1.0 for refinement passes where you trust the
first profile and want the second chart to densely sample the
printer's real gamut rather than empty corners of device space.

Tick the checkbox to enable.

title: Cube Interior Steps (-m)
body:
Adds a regular grid of patches *inside* the printer's colour
cube — N steps along each axis (N×N×N for RGB, etc.). These
are placed *in addition to* the patches you've chosen with
-f, -g, -s, and the other counters.

Set to 0 (default) to skip — almost always the right choice.
OFPS already covers the cube interior more efficiently.

When to use it:
  • Repeatability across machines: a fixed grid is the same
    every time, regardless of which OFPS placements targen
    picked, which can help compare profiles across runs.
  • Diagnostic charts where you want predictable, named cube
    positions.

Typical values when used: 3 – 6 (steps per axis). Numbers
grow fast — 6 steps in RGB is 216 patches, 8 is 512.

Tick the checkbox to enable.

title: Cube Surface Steps (-M)
body:
Adds a regular grid of patches on the *surface* of the printer's
colour cube — N steps along each face. Patches go on the
outside (primaries, secondaries, gamut edge) but not in the
interior.

Set to 0 (default) to skip.

When to use it:
  • You specifically want to nail down the gamut boundary and
    primary/secondary corners without the interior overhead
    of -m.
  • Comparing how different inks/papers shift the gamut
    envelope — surface patches are the ones most affected.

Typical values when used: 4 – 8 steps per face.

Tick the checkbox to enable.

title: Body-Centered Cubic Steps (-b)
body:
Adds patches on a body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice — denser
than a plain cube grid because it places points at both the
cube corners and the cube centres. N is the number of
subdivisions along each axis.

Set to 0 (default) to skip — this is a niche knob.

When to use it:
  • You want regular, lattice-aligned patch positions but
    with better packing than -m gives, without going all the
    way to OFPS.
  • Research / repeatability scenarios where the BCC structure
    itself is the point.

Note: this is the *step counter* form (adds to your patch list);
for a chart whose *entire* distribution is BCC, use the
"Patch Distribution" selector above and pick the body-centered
cubic option there.

Tick the checkbox to enable.

title: Edit patch recipe
body:
Edit the patch recipe (targen settings)

This preset comes with a ready-made set of colour patches, so the targen settings above are locked. Tick this box only if you really want to change which colours get printed.

Important: targen decides WHICH colours are on the chart. The moment you change anything here, ChromIQ can no longer reuse the preset's carefully chosen patches — it will build a brand-new set of colours from scratch. The chart is still perfectly valid, but it will NOT be the same as the preset, and the preset's hand-tuning no longer applies.

Leave this unticked unless you specifically need a different patch set.

title: Measurement Instrument (-i)
body:
Tells the chart generator which spectrophotometer you will use to
read the printed chart. The patch grid is built around that
instrument's strip width, patch size and spacing — so getting
this right is essential.

  •  i1Pro / i1Pro 2 / i1Pro 3 — handheld strip reader, the most
     common choice. Reads a column of patches in one sweep.

  •  i1Pro 3 Plus — larger-aperture version of the i1Pro 3.
     Reads bigger patches, so far fewer fit per sheet (~5× less
     than the regular i1Pro).

  •  ColorMunki / i1Studio / ColorChecker Studio — entry-level
     device. Reads one patch at a time on its own; with the
     optional measuring rig it pairs them up (see Double Density).

  •  SpectroScan — flatbed XY scanner. A motorised arm reads
     each patch individually, so it packs far more colours per
     sheet than any strip reader.

  •  CR30 (ChnSpec) — small hand-held colorimeter that reads
     ONE patch at a time. You place it on a patch and press the
     button on the instrument; ChromIQ records that patch and
     highlights the next one. The chart is a plain grid with row
     numbers and column letters so you can find the patch being
     asked for. Its patch size is PROVISIONAL (12 mm squares —
     a reasoned starting point, not a measured minimum), and each
     patch is a placement and a press of about two seconds, so a
     full A4 sheet of ~345 patches is a long sitting. A CR30 chart is
     ALWAYS laid out by ChromIQ's own layout engine, and can
     only be read by ChromIQ — standard ArgyllCMS chartread does
     not know this instrument and refuses the chart.

  •  i1iSis (via i1Profiler) — automatic sheet-fed chart reader.
     ChromIQ cannot drive this device directly: instead it will
     save the patch list in i1Profiler's own format alongside
     the chart, and you finish the workflow there (print, scan,
     build profile). ChromIQ's Print and Measure tabs are not
     used for this device.

Picking the wrong instrument produces a chart your

title: Double Density (-h)
body:
Doubles the number of patches that fit in each measurement strip when using a ColorMunki / i1Studio / ColorChecker Studio.

REQUIRES the physical measuring rig accessory — a clear plastic guide that mounts the instrument over the chart. Without the rig the device cannot align to the tighter patch spacing and will misread.

With the rig you get roughly twice as many patches per page, which means either a more detailed profile from the same number of sheets, or the same profile quality on fewer sheets. Recommended for anyone with the rig — it's a strict upgrade on patch density.

Has no effect on i1Pro, i1Pro 3 Plus or SpectroScan — the option is hidden when those are selected.

title: Triple Density (i1Pro layout emulation)
body:
ColorMunki + rig only. Generates the chart with the i1Pro strip layout (printtarg -ii1) plus the tuned scale / margin / strip-limit overrides needed for the ColorMunki to read it, then rewrites the produced .ti2 so chartread still talks to your ColorMunki. Result: roughly 3× the patch count of a plain ColorMunki chart at the same paper size.

REQUIRES the physical measuring rig accessory.

Mutually exclusive with Double density. Ticking this stashes the current -a / -m / -P widget values and sets them to the triple-density preset (1.3 / 5 / on); unticking restores the stashed values.

Has no effect on i1Pro, i1Pro 3 Plus or SpectroScan — the option is hidden when those are selected.

title: Paper Size (-p)
body:
Sets the dimensions of each sheet in the printed chart. The chart
always fills the page edge to edge — bigger paper fits more
patches, which means a more detailed profile from fewer sheets.

Pick the same size you will actually print on, including its
orientation. Strip readers (i1Pro family) read top-to-bottom, so:

  •  Portrait — longer strips, fewer of them. Standard choice.

  •  Landscape (A4R, LetterR, 420×297…) — shorter strips, more
     of them. Use this when your printer feeds landscape more
     reliably, or when a portrait sheet would leave the last
     strip too close to the paper edge.

Select "Custom" to enter exact width and height in millimetres
when none of the named sizes match the paper you're using.

If you change paper size, the patch count and page count in the
command preview update automatically.

title: TIFF Resolution (-t)
body:
Output resolution for the TIFF raster chart files.
300 DPI is recommended for strip-reading instruments and gives
a good balance of file size and patch clarity.
Use 200 DPI for very large charts to reduce file size.
Higher values (600+) are rarely needed and produce large files.

title: Suppress Left Clip Border (-L)
body:
Removes the left-edge paper-clip border strip, reclaiming
~15 mm of page width for additional patch columns.
Enable this unless you are using a physical page-clamp jig.
All values in the patch database assume this flag is ON.

title: Patch Size Scale (-a)
body:
Scales the patch and spacer dimensions uniformly.
1.0 is the default (instrument-optimised size).
Increase to 1.5–2.0 on rough / textured papers where the
instrument needs a larger measurement area.
Decreasing below 1.0 fits more patches per page but may
cause read errors on some instruments.
Note: changing this value from the default triggers a
live binary-search recalculation instead of the fast lookup.

title: Declare Extra Inks as Alpha Channels (-N)
body:
Only for charts with more than four inks, and only if the
software you hand the TIFF to asks for it.

A TIFF says what its first channels are, but has no standard
way to name a fifth, sixth or seventh ink.  This option marks
the extra ones as "alpha" channels, which is the flag some
RIPs look for.

EVERY INK IS WRITTEN TO THE FILE EITHER WAY.  This changes how
they are labelled, not what is in them, and ChromIQ's own
printing does not need it.

Leave it off unless your RIP's documentation asks for the
extra inks to be declared.  Some readers treat an alpha
channel as transparency rather than ink, so switching it on
blindly can do more harm than leaving it alone.

title: Pages (Auto patch count)
body:
How many physical sheets the chart should span. This control drives the Auto checkbox next to targen → Total Patch Count above: when Auto is on, ChromIQ picks the patch count that fills exactly this many sheets — using the current paper, instrument, double-density / hexagon, left-border, patch scale and margin settings. Total patches = patches-per-page × pages.

More pages means more colour samples, which produces a more accurate profile. The trade-off is more ink, more paper and a longer reading session. Rough guide:

  •  1 page — quick check or single-sheet workflows (~500 patches on A4 with an i1Pro). Fine for casual profiling.

  •  2-3 pages — recommended for everyday photo printing. Good balance of accuracy versus effort.

  •  4-5+ pages — professional or fine-art workflows where the profile needs to nail tricky tonal transitions and out-of-gamut colours.

This control is greyed out when Auto is off — without Auto, printtarg just uses as many sheets as the explicit Total Patch Count requires.

title: Margin (-m / -M)
body:
Sets the margin in millimetres for both the printable area (-m)
and the TIFF file dimensions (-M).  Both are kept in sync.
6 mm matches most printer minimum margins.  Reduce only if
your printer supports borderless printing.

Selecting an i1Pro / i1Pro 2 / i1Pro 3 / i1Pro 3 Plus instrument
auto-bumps this to 10 mm so the strip-reader optics don't drift
onto the bare paper edge ("not enough patches read" errors).
Switching to ColorMunki / SpectroScan returns it to 6 mm. A
custom value (anything other than 6 or 10) is preserved across
instrument changes.

Patch-per-page lookup tables exist for 6 and 10 mm only — other
values trigger a live binary-search recalculation.

title: No Randomisation (-r)
body:
By default printtarg randomises patch positions to reduce
instrument drift artefacts.  Enable this flag only if you
are testing a specific patch sequence or if your instrument
requires ordered patches.

title: Force B&W Spacers (-b)
body:
Forces inter-strip spacers to be black/white instead of
coloured.  Does not affect patch count or layout geometry.

Has no effect when "No Spacers" (-n) is enabled — this option
is greyed out and excluded from the printtarg command in that
case.

title: Don't Limit Strip Length (-P)
body:
By default printtarg caps strip length so that every strip
fits within the paper without overflow.  Enabling this flag
removes that limit, allowing very long strips.
Useful for narrow roll paper or when you want as few strips
as possible for a given patch count.
Warning: if the patch count is high, strips may extend
beyond the paper edge — verify the generated TIFF before
printing.

title: Apply Calibration to Patches (-K)
body:
Use this when your printer has no built-in calibration system
— i.e. the printer driver or RIP cannot apply a calibration
curve on its own.

You first run Argyll's printcal to produce a .cal file that
describes how to linearise the printer.  Then you pass that
.cal here: printtarg remaps every patch colour value through
the calibration curves before generating the chart, so the
printed target already reflects calibrated device behaviour.
The .cal is also embedded in the .ti2 file so that colprof
can reference it when building the ICC profile.

Typical use: desktop inkjet printers without built-in
linearisation, driven directly from a TIFF with no
intervening RIP.

Mutually exclusive with "Include Calibration" (-I) — only
one calibration option can be active at a time.

title: Include Calibration Without Applying (-I)
body:
Use this when your printer or RIP already applies a
calibration curve natively — for example, a production inkjet
RIP with its own linearisation LUT, or a printer with
built-in density calibration.

In this case you do not want printtarg to remap the patch
values (the printer handles that itself), but you do want
colprof to know about the calibration.  -I embeds the .cal
file into the .ti2 output as metadata only, leaving all patch
values untouched.

Typical use: professional inkjet RIPs (e.g. EFI Fiery,
Wasatch, ColorBurst) or printers with built-in linearisation
that is active during the profiling print run.

Mutually exclusive with "Apply Calibration" (-K) — only one
calibration option can be active at a time.

title: Disable TIFF Compression (-C)
body:
Outputs uncompressed TIFF files instead of the default LZW
compression.  Uncompressed files are larger but universally
compatible with all RIPs and printer drivers.
Enable this if your print workflow refuses or mangles
compressed TIFFs.

title: Dither 8-bit Output (-D)
body:
When generating an 8-bit TIFF, uses error-diffusion dithering
to down-sample from internal 16-bit precision.  This reduces
banding in smooth gradients that would otherwise be caused by
quantisation.
Only has an effect when 8-bit TIFF output is selected.

title: Suppress CUPS CMM Header (-U)
body:
Removes the 'cupsJobTicket: cups-disable-cmm' comment from
PostScript and EPS output files.  Some CUPS versions react
differently to this comment.
This option only affects PS/EPS output and has no effect on
TIFF files.  Enable only if you are experiencing unexpected
colour management being applied during printing.

title: Randomisation Seed (-R)
body:
Sets the starting seed for the patch randomisation algorithm.
Using the same seed with the same patch count always produces
the same patch layout, making charts fully reproducible.
Useful for research or when you need to regenerate an
identical chart at a later date.
Has no effect when "Preserve Patch Order" (-r) is enabled.

title: Quantize Patch Values (-Q)
body:
Rounds all patch colour values to fit within the specified
bit depth before generating the chart.  For example, -Q 8
rounds all values to 8-bit (256-level) precision.
Use this when your printer pipeline introduces banding at a
specific bit depth and you want to test at exactly that
precision level.

title: Spacer-Only Scale (-A)
body:
Applies an additional scaling factor to the spacer bars only,
without changing the patch dimensions set by -a.
Values above 1.0 make spacers wider; below 1.0 make them
narrower.  Useful for instruments that need extra separation
between strips or when you want to reclaim space by narrowing
spacers while keeping patch size constant.

Has no effect when "No Spacers" (-n) is enabled — this option
is greyed out and excluded from the printtarg command in that
case.

title: No Spacers (-n)
body:
Removes all spacer bars between patches and strips.  Spacers
normally help the instrument identify strip boundaries and
direction.
Disable spacers only if your measurement workflow explicitly
does not rely on them (e.g. some flatbed scanner setups).

When enabled, "Force B&W Spacers" (-b) and "Spacer-Only Scale"
(-A) are automatically disabled since both only affect spacers.

title: Force Colored Spacers (-c)
body:
Forces inter-patch spacer areas to be rendered in colour
rather than the default (which may be black/white depending
on the instrument profile).  Can improve strip recognition
on some colour inkjet devices where black spacers have low
contrast against dark patches.

title: Edit page layout
body:
Edit the page layout (printtarg settings)

This preset is already arranged on the page for you, so the printtarg settings above are locked. Tick this box if you'd like to re-arrange the same patches differently — for example a different paper size, margin or patch size.

Good news: changing only these layout settings keeps the preset's exact colour patches. ChromIQ simply re-lays that same set of colours onto the page using your new settings.

(To change the colours themselves, use the "Edit patch recipe" box on the targen panel instead — but note that produces a different, non-matching set of patches.)

title: Instrument
body: The measuring device you'll read the printed chart with. It sets the patch size, strip length and overall layout the chart is built for, so pick the one you actually own — a chart laid out for one instrument may not read correctly on another.

title: Paper and pages
body: Paper is the sheet size you'll print on — the profile is only valid for the paper you actually use. Pages is how many sheets to spread the patches across: more pages = more patches total (and more ink and paper).

title: Create layout
body:
Two ways to decide patch size against how many fit. Whichever you pick, its own settings appear directly below this box.

• Prioritise patch size — you set the patch size, or a scale to grow and shrink the instrument's standard size, and ChromIQ fits as many patches as it can. Simple, but the last strip may not reach the far margin. Leave the size on “auto” and ChromIQ uses the size your instrument prefers.

• Prioritise chart area — you decide the GRID and ChromIQ sizes the patches so it fills the space inside your margins. Two ways to describe the grid: by patch width, where you give the smallest patch you are willing to read and ChromIQ fits as many as that allows; or by columns and rows, where you say how many strips and how many patches per strip you want. Either way the patch area lands exactly where you defined it, and you trade patch size for the grid you asked for. Watch that the patches don't get too small for your instrument to read.

title: Patch size
body:
Width × height of each patch in millimetres. Leave at “auto” (0) to use the instrument's recommended size (scaled by Patch scale). A value below ~6 mm can make the chart hard to read.

Hexagonal patches have two heights, and they are not the same number.
Hexagons interlock, so a row of them starts before the row above has finished and the patches sit closer together than they are tall. The ROW PITCH is that closer spacing, centre to centre down a strip. It decides how many patches fit on the page, and it is the height you set in the Patch size boxes. The PATCH is the hexagon itself, measured top tip to bottom tip, and it is a third taller: set 9.78 mm and you get a patch 13.05 mm from tip to tip, taller than it is wide. Chart layout information shows you both.

title: Patch scale
body: Grows or shrinks every patch (and its spacer) together. 1.0 is the instrument's standard size. Below 1.0 fits more patches per sheet but each is harder for the instrument to read reliably — watch the warning if patches get too small.

title: Calculation method
body:
How to work out the patch grid inside the area:

• By patch width — you set the smallest patch width (and a height %); ChromIQ fits as many as possible at that size and grows them to fill the area. You know the strip width you want, without juggling column counts.

• By columns / rows — you set exactly how many strips and patches-per-strip; ChromIQ sizes the patches to fit. Full control of the grid, but you tune the counts to land on a patch size you like.

Both fill the same patch area defined by the margins.

title: Minimum patch width
body: The smallest strip (patch) width your instrument can read reliably. ChromIQ fits as many strips as possible at this width, then grows them slightly so the grid fills the area exactly. The patch height follows the height % below.

title: Minimum patch height
body: The patch height as a percentage of its width. 100% keeps height = width (square); 150% makes each patch half again as tall as it is wide; below 100% makes them wider than tall. It's a minimum — the engine grows the patches from here to fill the chart area.

title: Strips (columns)
body:
How many strips (columns of patches) to fit across the page. ChromIQ makes the patches exactly wide enough that this many strips span the usable width, so the block reaches the margins evenly.

Leave it on “auto” and ChromIQ picks a count that gives a patch close to your instrument's natural patch size — the size it was designed to read — then fills the width to that count.

title: Patches per strip (rows)
body:
How many patches to stack down each strip. ChromIQ makes the patches exactly tall enough that this many fit the usable height.

Leave it on “auto” and ChromIQ picks a count that gives a patch close to your instrument's natural patch size — the size it was designed to read — then fills the height to that count.

title: Strip indicators
body:
The small label printed above each strip so you always know which strip you're measuring and in what order. They are usually letters (A, B, C…), and they follow the chart's own strip pattern, so a chart set to numbers is labelled 1, 2, 3 instead. Turn off only if you have another way to keep the strips straight.

Where they sit. They hang from the top edge of the paper at the distance you set in “Top” under “Text distance from edge”, and they never slide down into the patches. If the top margin is too small to hold a whole label, the label moves up towards the paper edge rather than over the first row. Example, A4 portrait with “Top” at 4 mm and letters about 7 mm tall: with a 15 mm top margin the letters are printed between 4 mm and 11 mm from the top edge, leaving 4 mm of air above the first row of patches. Narrow the top margin to 10 mm and there is no longer room for both, so the letters move up to between 3 mm and 10 mm, which is closer to the paper edge than the 4 mm you asked for, and that is reported under the preview.

The band is as tall as the letters at the size you chose and it lives inside the top margin, so switching this on can leave room for fewer or slightly smaller patches. If the top margin cannot hold it, that is reported under the preview.

The row indicators down the left-hand side work the same way, with “Clip” in place of “Top”. Their own help has the arithmetic. Set the font, size and underline style in Preferences → Chart Layout.

title: Row indicators
body:
Prints a label down the left-hand side of the chart for every row of patches. They are usually numbers (1, 2, 3…), and they follow whatever the chart's own patch pattern says, so a chart set to letters is labelled A, B, C instead. Together with the strip letters along the top it gives the sheet a two-way coordinate, so a patch can be found the way a square is found on a map: strip A, row 12.

This is most useful when you place the instrument on one patch at a time, such as a SpectroScan or a CR30, which is why those two have always printed it. You can also switch the strip letters off and keep only these, which is what you want when every patch is read on its own. Turn it on for any chart you want to read by hand, or off to get the space back.

Where the labels sit. They start at a fixed distance from the left edge of the paper, and you choose that distance yourself with “Clip” under “Text distance from edge”. If the chart has a clip border down the same edge, the labels start at the border's width instead whenever that is the larger of the two, so the border cannot be printed on top of them. The band itself is as wide as the widest label at the size you chose, plus 1 mm of air to the left of the text.

How much paper it takes. The left margin has to hold the whole band, so ChromIQ widens it when the one you asked for is too narrow. The width it needs is the starting distance, plus the width of the label text, plus 1 mm before it and 1 mm after it. Two worked examples, both A4 portrait:
  •  No clip border, “Clip” set to 4 mm, two-digit numbers about 5 mm wide. The labels start 4 mm in from the paper edge, the band is 6 mm wide, and the patches start at 11 mm. Ask for a 6 mm left margin and you get 11 mm.
  •  A 26 mm clip border on the left, the same labels. The labels start at 26 mm, because the border is wider than “Clip”, and the patches start at 33 mm. Ask for a 26 mm left margin and you get 33 mm.
Whenever the margin is widened like that, it is reported under

title: Clip border
body: Whether a CLIP BORDER is printed — the white strip the measuring rail grips so it can pull the chart through. Turning it off frees that space for more patches; only do so if your rig doesn't need it. Choose which edge it sits on, and what it carries (a notes box, text or a logo), in the Clip-border content section.

title: Clip border
body:
Reserve a clip-border strip on this chart (the same option the i1Pro has). On reserves a band you can fill with a notes box, text or a logo in the Clip-border content section below; Off uses the whole page for patches. Choose which edge it sits on in that section.

If you also print the ruler helper markers (the short dashes along the page edges, switched on under the preview), a dash can cross this band. That is allowed on purpose — the dashes keep step with the patches wherever they fall. If one lands awkwardly, move it with its own “Distance from page edge”, or make it shorter.

title: Offset every second strip
body: ColorMunki only: shifts every second strip down by half a patch so the columns interleave like a brick wall — matching ArgyllCMS printtarg's measuring-rig layout. Reserves a little space at the top and bottom for the offset, so the patch count drops slightly. Leave off for a plain aligned grid.

title: Randomisation
body: Patches are shuffled across the sheet so a streak of similar colours can't bias a strip — leave this on. The seed is the number that drives the shuffle: with a fixed seed the exact same layout is reproduced every build (handy for re-printing an identical chart), otherwise a fresh seed is drawn each time. Press New seed to draw one now; it's saved with the chart so you can always recreate it. After every build the Seed box shows the number the chart on screen was shuffled with, even while the box is greyed out — tick “Use a fixed seed” to build that exact layout again.

title: Use instrument margins
body: Fill the four page margins from the per-instrument minimums set in Preferences → Instrument Limits for this instrument and paper, and lock them so the patch area always clears your reading jig. They refill automatically when you change instrument or paper. Untick to type your own margins.

title: Margins
body:
Blank borders kept clear of patches on each edge — Top, Right, Bottom, Left, in mm. Most printers can't print to the very edge, so keep a few mm here; the smallest of the four also sets the instrument's leader/clip base.

When the clip border is on, the margin on the clip edge (Left or Right, set by “Side” under Clip-border content) shares that edge with the clip-border width: the larger of the two is what's reserved. If the clip-border width is wider than this margin, it wins and the margin box is outlined in red to show it's being overridden.

title: Clip border width
body:
Width of the clip border — the blank band reserved down one edge of the page for the clip that holds the sheet against the scanner bed. Make it wider if your clip covers more of the page; the patches start just past it. Only applies to the i1Pro / i1Pro 3 in clip-border mode (printtarg fixes this at 26 mm).

Works together with the page margin on the same edge (Left or Right, set by “Side” under Clip-border content): the reserved clip zone is whichever of the two is larger. If that margin is wider than this width, the margin wins and this value is ignored — the box is outlined in red to show it. Raise this above the margin to make the clip zone wider than the margin.

title: Resolution
body: Pixel density of the printed chart TIFF, in dots per inch. 300 dpi is a good default; higher makes a larger file with no real benefit for solid colour patches.

title: Max strip length
body: Caps how long a single strip (column of patches) may get, in mm. Leave at “auto” to use the instrument's limit (set per instrument/paper in Preferences → Instrument Limits). Some scanners can't read a strip past a certain length; lower this if long strips misread. Only used in “Prioritise patch size” — area-first fills the page and warns if a strip is longer than the instrument's ruler instead.

title: Chart offset
body: Shifts the whole patch block right (X) and down (Y) on the sheet, in mm. Usually 0 — use it to nudge the layout away from a printer's unprintable area or to line up with a pre-printed sheet. Only used in “Prioritise patch size”; area-first places the block by the margins.

title: Strip pattern
body:
How each strip (column of patches) is labelled — the first part of a patch's location, e.g. the “A” in A12. ChromIQ reads this the way ArgyllCMS's printtarg does; in practice it decides whether strips are labelled with LETTERS or NUMBERS.

Valid examples:
• A-Z, A-Z — the default: letters A, B, C … Z, then AA, AB, AC … once past 26 strips (like spreadsheet columns).
• A-Z — plain letters A, B, C … (same result while a chart has 26 strips or fewer).
• 1-999 — numbers 1, 2, 3 …
• 0-9 — also numbers 1, 2, 3 …

Rule: any pattern that contains “A-Z” labels with letters; anything else counts in plain numbers (no zero-padding). This works together with the Patch pattern below — the two combine into each location label, strip then patch (e.g. strip “A” + patch “12” = A12). Leave the default unless you're matching a specific reading-sheet scheme.

title: Patch pattern
body:
How patches within a strip are labelled — the second part of a location, e.g. the “12” in A12. The patch label is joined to the strip label to form each patch's full location (strip then patch, e.g. A12).

The one rule that always applies: if the pattern contains “A-Z” you get LETTERS, otherwise you get NUMBERS.

Common patterns:
• 0-9,@-9,@-9;1-999 — the default: numbers 1, 2, 3 …
• 1-999 — numbers 1, 2, 3 … (simpler, same result).
• A-Z, A-Z — letters A, B, C … Z, AA, AB ….
• A-Z — plain letters A, B, C ….

About the “@” and zeros (ArgyllCMS notation, used by the classic printtarg engine):
• “@” means “this digit may be left blank”. It is what stops the default from writing leading zeros — you get 1, 2, … 9, 10 rather than 001, 002 …
• To start counting at 0 instead of 1, include 0 in the range, e.g. 0-999 → 0, 1, 2 ….
• To keep every number the same width WITH leading zeros (01, 02, … 09, 10), use a fixed-width digit range such as 00-99 (two digits) or 000-999 (three).

Note: ChromIQ's own layout engine keeps patch numbers simple (1, 2, 3 …) whatever the digit details; the “@” and leading-zero options above take effect when a chart is built with the classic printtarg engine. Leave the default unless you're matching a specific scheme.

title: Patch area alignment
body:
Where the whole patch block sits within the page once the margins are kept clear. The patches rarely fill the usable area exactly, so this decides where the leftover white space goes.

“Top-left” pins the block to the top-left corner (the leftover sits at the right and bottom); “Centre” puts the spare space evenly around it; “Bottom-right” pins it to the opposite corner, and so on. It only moves the block — the patch count and size don't change. Margins / thresholds are still respected.

title: Don't cap strip length
body: Removes the strip-length limit entirely (printtarg -P), letting a strip run the full usable height. Only enable if your instrument can read an unlimited-length strip; otherwise leave it off. Only used in “Prioritise patch size” — area-first already fills the page, so it's hidden there.

title: Spacers
body: The thin separator drawn between patches in a strip so the instrument can tell where one patch ends and the next begins. “Coloured” picks a high-contrast colour per gap (default, most reliable); “Black & white” uses plain black/white; “None” removes them — only if your instrument doesn't need gaps.

title: Spacer size
body: How thick the separator between patches is, in mm (it runs along the strip, between consecutive patches). Leave at “auto” (0) for the instrument default; increase it only if your scanner has trouble finding the patch edges.

title: Spacer scale
body: Scales only the spacer thickness, leaving patch size alone. 1.0 is standard; raise it for fatter gaps without making the patches bigger.

title: Inter-patch gap
body: Makes the spacer between patches thicker, in mm — extra blank separation along the strip. Usually 0; raise it only if patches bleed into each other on your printer/paper.

title: Strip-indicator gap
body: How far the strip's letter label sits below the top edge of the page, in mm. At 0 the labels hug the minimum text-edge distance at the very top; raising it slides them down, toward the patches, to fine-tune where the labels print.

title: Strip gap
body: Extra blank space added sideways between neighbouring strips (columns of patches), in mm. Usually 0, which packs the strips as tightly as the instrument allows to fit the most patches per sheet. Raise it if your scanner needs a wider gutter between strips, or to spread a sparse chart out — each millimetre here means fewer strips fit, so the patch count drops.

title: Custom spacer colours
body: By default the engine separates patches with spacers drawn from the five ChromIQ accent colours plus white and black, automatically picking the one with the most contrast at each gap so the instrument can always find the patch edges (white and black give it a strong choice against very dark or very light patches). Turn this on to choose your own set instead — click a swatch to change it. The engine still auto-picks the highest-contrast one from your set per gap, so keep them varied (and watch the low-contrast warning).

title: Edge spacers
body: Adds a spacer before the first patch and after the last patch of every strip — the way ArgyllCMS printtarg does. It's optional: the instrument finds each strip from the white border the layout already leaves at both ends, so this isn't needed for reliable reading. It fits in space the layout already reserves, so it doesn't reduce the patch count. Turn it on if you prefer the printtarg look or want an extra separator at the strip ends.

title: Bit depth
body: Colour precision of the chart TIFF. 8-bit is standard and right for almost everyone. 16-bit doubles the file size and only helps if your whole print path is genuinely 16-bit — otherwise it makes no visible difference.

title: Compression
body: How the chart TIFF is compressed. LZW (default) and Zlib are lossless and shrink the file; “None” writes it uncompressed (largest, most compatible). All keep the exact colours.

title: Also export a PDF
body:
Saves a press-ready PDF of the chart next to the usual TIFF — the TIFF is still made, this just adds a PDF copy.

When it helps:
• Your print shop or RIP prefers PDF, or asks for one.
• You want a file that prints at the exact paper size, with no print dialog quietly scaling it down.
• Multi-ink charts (CMYK and CMYK + extra inks): the PDF carries each ink as its own named channel, so a RIP knows exactly which ink is which.

The PDF is drawn as true vector — the patches are exact device colours and the labels stay crisp at any zoom — and it uses the same fonts as the chart. All pages are in one file.

One rule matters more than the rest: nothing between this file and the paper may convert the colours. That is not the same advice as for the TIFF, and the reason is in the PDF format rather than in any one system. Both files hold raw device values with no colour profile attached, which is what a chart needs — but where a TIFF is a picture whose numbers get passed along, a PDF lets whatever opens it decide that those numbers meant some particular colour space, and convert them. Measured on macOS, a pure red patch of 255,0,0 came back as 234,51,35. On Linux, the PDF interpreter behind most print queues assigns a default colour profile unless it is told not to. On Windows it depends entirely on the application you print from. How far the colours move depends on the machine and the program, so the same file can look fine on one and be badly wrong on another.

None of which means a chart PDF cannot be printed properly — it can, and there are three ways to be sure of it:
• Send it straight to the print queue, which is what ChromIQ does with its own charts.
• Give it to a RIP with colour management switched off — what this export is really for.
• Print from an application with an explicit setting for it, such as “Same as source (no colour management)”.
